entries.d069aae0b67ecdb9a02cc59a75ccc70b73178064: <div sID="gen33476" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="1Pet.4" sID="1Pet.4"/> <div eID="gen33476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33477" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33478" type="x-p"/> The work of a Christian is twofold—doing the will of God and suffering his pleasure. This chapter directs us in both. The duties we are here exhorted to employ ourselves in are the mortification of sin, living to God, sobriety, prayer, charity, hospitality, and the best improvement of our talents, which the apostle presses upon Christians from the consideration of the time they have lost in their sins, and the approaching end of all things, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.1-1Pet.4.11">ver. 1-11</reference>. The directions for sufferings are that we should not be surprised at them, but rejoice in them, only take care not to suffer as evil-doers. He intimates that their trials were near at hand, that their souls were in danger as well as their bodies, and that the best way to preserve their souls is to commit them to God in well-doing.
entries.c5dcd9649a632542ccfe1cfeaf66363c50d6619f: <div eID="gen33478" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33477" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Mortification of Sin. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen33479" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Forasmuch then as Christ hath suffered for us in the flesh, arm yourselves likewise with the same mind: for he that hath suffered in the flesh hath ceased from sin; <hi type="super">2</hi> That he no longer should live the rest of <hi type="italic">his</hi> time in the flesh to the lusts of men, but to the will of God. <hi type="super">3</hi> For the time past of <hi type="italic">our</hi> life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries: <div eID="gen33479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33480" type="x-p"/> The apostle here draws a new inference from the consideration of Christ's sufferings. As he had before made use of it to persuade to patience in suffering, so here to mortification of sin. Observe, <div eID="gen33480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33481" type="x-p"/> I. How the exhortation is expressed. The antecedent or supposition is <hi type="italic">that Christ had suffered</hi> for us in the flesh, or in his human nature. The consequent or inference is, "<hi type="italic">Arm</hi> and fortify <hi type="italic">yourselves likewise with the same mind,</hi> courage, and resolution." The word flesh in the former part of the verse signifies Christ's human nature, but in the latter part it signifies man's corrupt nature. So the sense is, "As Christ suffered in his human nature, do you, according to your baptismal vow and profession, make your corrupt nature suffer, by putting to death the body of sin by self-denial and mortification; for, if you do not thus suffer, you will be conformable to Christ in his death and resurrection, and will cease <hi type="italic">from sin.</hi>" Learn, 1. Some of the strongest and best arguments against all sorts of sin are taken from the sufferings of Christ. All sympathy and tenderness for Christ as a sufferer are lost of you do not put away sin. He dies to destroy it; and, though he could cheerfully submit to the worst sufferings, yet he could never submit to the least sin. 2. The beginning of all true mortification lies in the mind, not in penances and hardships upon the body. The mind of man is carnal, full of enmity; the understanding is darkened, being alienated from the life of God, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.18">Eph. iv. 18</reference>. Man is not a sincere creature, but partial, blind, and wicked, till he be renewed and sanctifies by the regenerating grace of God. <div eID="gen33481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33482" type="x-p"/> II. How it is further explained, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.2">v. 2</reference>. The apostle explains what he means by being dead to sin, and ceasing from sin, both negatively and positively. Negatively, a Christian ought <hi type="italic">no longer to live the rest of his time in the flesh,</hi> to the sinful lusts and corrupt desires of carnal wicked men; but, positively, he ought to conform himself to the revealed will of the holy God. Learn, 1. The lusts of men are the springs of all their wickedness, <reference osisRef="Jas.1.13-Jas.1.14">Jam. i. 13, 14</reference>. Let occasional temptations be what they will, they could not prevail, were it not for men's own corruptions. 2. All good Christians make the will of God, not their own lusts or desires, the rule of their lives and actions. 3. True conversion makes a marvellous change in the heart and life of every one who partakes of it. It brings a man off from all his old, fashionable, and delightful lusts, and from the common ways and vices of the world, to the will of God. It alters the mind, judgment, affections, way, and conversation of every one who has experienced it. <div eID="gen33482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33483" type="x-p"/> III. How it is enforced (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">For the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles,</hi> &c. Here the apostle argues from equity. "It is but just, equal, and reasonable, that as you have hitherto all the former part of your life served sin and Satan, so you should now serve the living God." Though those were Jews to whom the apostle wrote, yet the living among the Gentiles they had learned their way. Observe, 1. When a man is truly converted, it is very grievous to him to think how the time past of his life has been spent; the hazard he has run so many years, the mischief he has done to others, the dishonour done to God, and the loss he has sustained, are very afflicting to him. 2. While the will of man is unsanctified and corrupt, he walks continually in wicked ways; he makes them his choice and delight, his work and business, and he makes a bad condition daily worse and worse. 3. One sin, allowed, draws on another. Here are six named, and they have a connection and dependence one upon another. (1.) <hi type="italic">Lasciviousness</hi> or wantonness, expressed in looks, gesture, or behaviour, <reference osisRef="Rom.13.13">Rom. xiii. 13</reference>. (2.) <hi type="italic">Lusts,</hi> acts of lewdness, such as whoredom and adultery. (3.) <hi type="italic">Excess of wine,</hi> though short of drunkenness, an immoderate use of it, to the prejudice of health or business, is here condemned. (4.) <hi type="italic">Revellings,</hi> or luxurious feastings, too frequent, too full, or too expensive. (5.) <hi type="italic">Banquetings,</hi> by which is meant gluttony or excess in eating. (6.) <hi type="italic">Abominable</hi> idolatry; the idol-worship of the Gentiles was attended with lewdness, drunkenness, gluttony, and all sorts of brutality and cruelty; and these Jews living long among them were, some of them at least, debauched and corrupted by such practices. 4. It is a Christian's duty not only to abstain from what is grossly wicked, but also from those things that are generally the occasions of sin, or carry the appearance of evil. <hi type="italic">Excess of wine</hi> and immoderate feasting are forbidden as well as lust and idolatry.
entries.1360980cead74c90e8dd7bb9292087748673a859: <div eID="gen33483" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Comfort of the Servants of God. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen33484" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Wherein they think it strange that ye run not with <hi type="italic">them</hi> to the same excess of riot, speaking evil of <hi type="italic">you:</hi> <hi type="super">5</hi> Who shall give account to him that is ready to judge the quick and the dead. <hi type="super">6</hi> For for this cause was the gospel preached also to them that are dead, that they might be judged according to men in the flesh, but live according to God in the spirit. <div eID="gen33484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33485" type="x-p"/> I. Here you have the visible change wrought in those who in the <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.3">foregoing verse</reference> were represented as having been in the former part of their life very wicked. They no longer run on in the same courses, or with the same companions, as they used to do. Hereupon observe the conduct of their wicked acquaintance towards them. 1. <hi type="italic">They think it strange,</hi> they are surprised and wonder at it, as at something new and unusual, that their old friends should be so much altered, and not run with as much violence as they used to do <hi type="italic">to the same excess of riot,</hi> to the same sottish excesses and luxury which before they had greedily and madly followed. 2. <hi type="italic">They speak evil of them.</hi> Their surprise carries them to blasphemy. They speak evil of their persons, of their way, their religion, and their God. Learn, (1.) Those that are once really converted will not return to their former course of life, though ever so much tempted by the frowns or flatteries of others to do so. Neither persuasion nor reproach will prevail with them to be or to do as they were wont to do. (2.) The temper and behaviour of true Christians seem very strange to ungodly men. That they should despise that which every one else is fond of, that they should believe many things which to others seem incredible, that they should delight in what is irksome and tedious, be zealous where they have no visible interest to serve, and depend so much upon hope, is what the ungodly cannot comprehend. (3.) The best actions of religious people cannot escape the censures and slanders of those who are irreligious. Those actions which cost a good man the most pains, hazard, and self-denial, shall be most censured by the uncharitable and ill-natured world; they will speak evil of good people, though they themselves reap the fruits of their charity, piety, and goodness. <div eID="gen33485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33486" type="x-p"/> II. For the comfort of the servants of God, it is here added, <div eID="gen33486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33487" type="x-p"/> 1. That all wicked people, especially those who speak evil of such as are not as bad as themselves, shall <hi type="italic">give an account,</hi> and be put to give a reason of their behaviour, to him who is ready to judge, who is both able and duly authorized, and who will ere long judge and pass sentence upon all who shall then be found alive, and all such as being dead shall then be raised again, <reference osisRef="Jas.5.8-Jas.5.9">Jam. v. 8, 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.7">2 Pet. iii. 7</reference>. Observe, The malignant world shall in a little time give an account to the great God of all their evil speeches against his people, <reference osisRef="Jude.1.14-Jude.1.15">Jude 14, 15</reference>. They will soon be called to a sad account for all their curses, their foolish jests, their slanders and falsehoods, uttered against the faithful people of God. <div eID="gen33487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33488" type="x-p"/> 2. That <hi type="italic">for this cause was the gospel preached also to those that are dead, that they might be judged according to men in the flesh, but live according to God in the Spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.6">v. 6</reference>. Some understand this difficult place thus: <hi type="italic">For this cause was the gospel preached</hi> to all the faithful of old, who are now dead in Christ, that thereby they might be taught and encouraged to bear the unrighteous judgments and persecutions which the rage of men put upon them <hi type="italic">in the flesh, but might live in the Spirit unto God.</hi> Others take the expression, <hi type="italic">that they might be judged according to men in the flesh,</hi> in a spiritual sense, thus: The gospel was preached to them, to judge them, condemn them, and reprove them, for the corruption of their natures, and the viciousness of their lives, while they lived after the manner of the heathen or the mere natural man; and that, having thus mortified their sins, they might live according to God, a new and spiritual life. Take it thus; and thence learn, 1. The mortifying of our sins and living to God are the expected effects of the gospel preached to us. 2. God will certainly reckon with all those who have had the gospel preached to them, but without these good effects produced by it. God is ready to judge all those who have received the gospel in vain. 3. It is no matter how we are judged according to men in the flesh, if we do but live according to God in the Spirit.
entries.79db15aecc8e4147a1650ec9adb6441547adce7b: <div eID="gen33488" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Sobriety, Watchfulness, and Charity; Improvement of Talents. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen33489" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> But the end of all things is at hand: be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer. <hi type="super">8</hi> And above all things have fervent charity among yourselves: for charity shall cover the multitude of sins. <hi type="super">9</hi> Use hospitality one to another without grudging. <hi type="super">10</hi> As every man hath received the gift, <hi type="italic">even so</hi> minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God. <hi type="super">11</hi> If any man speak, <hi type="italic">let him speak</hi> as the oracles of God; if any man minister, <hi type="italic">let him do it</hi> as of the ability which God giveth: that God in all things may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom be praise and dominion for ever and ever. Amen. <div eID="gen33489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33490" type="x-p"/> We have here an awful position or doctrine, and an inference drawn from it. The position is that the <hi type="italic">end of all things is at hand.</hi> The miserable destruction of the Jewish church and nation foretold by our Saviour is now very near; consequently, the time of their persecution and your sufferings is but very short. Your own life and that of your enemies will soon come to their utmost period. Nay, the world itself will not continue very long. The conflagration will put an end to it; and all things must be swallowed up in an endless eternity. The inference from this comprises a series of exhortations. <div eID="gen33490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33491" type="x-p"/> 1. To sobriety and watchfulness: "<hi type="italic">Be you therefore sober,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.7">v. 7</reference>. Let the frame and temper of your minds be grave, stayed, and solid; and observe strict temperance and sobriety in the use of all worldly enjoyments. Do not suffer yourselves to be caught with your former sins and temptations, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.3">v. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">An watch unto prayer.</hi> Take care that you be continually in a calm sober disposition, fit for prayer; and that you be frequent in prayers, lest this end come upon you unawares," <reference osisRef="Luke.21.34">Luke xxi. 34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.26.40-Matt.26.41">Matt. xxvi. 40, 41</reference>. Learn, (1.) The consideration of our approaching end is a powerful argument to make us sober in all worldly matters, and earnest in religious affairs. (2.) Those who would pray to purpose must <hi type="italic">watch unto prayer.</hi> They must watch over their own spirits, watch all fit opportunities, and do their duty in the best manner they can. (3.) The right ordering of the body is of great use to promote the good of the soul. When the appetites and inclinations of the body are restrained and governed by God's word and true reason, and the interests of the body are submitted to the interests and necessities of the soul, then it is not the soul's enemy, but its friend and helper. <div eID="gen33491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33492" type="x-p"/> 2. To charity: <hi type="italic">And above all things have fervent charity among yourselves,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.8">v. 8</reference>. Here is a noble rule in Christianity. Christians ought to love one another, which implies an affection to their persons, a desire of their welfare, and a hearty endeavour to promote it. This mutual affection must not be cold, but fervent, that is, sincere, strong, and lasting. This sort of earnest affection is recommended <hi type="italic">above all things,</hi> which shows the importance of it, <reference osisRef="Col.3.14">Col. iii. 14</reference>. It is greater than faith or hope, <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.13">1 Cor. xiii. 13</reference>. One excellent effect of it is that it will <hi type="italic">cover a multitude of sins.</hi> Learn, (1.) There ought to be in all Christians a more fervent charity towards one another than towards other men: <hi type="italic">Have charity among yourselves.</hi> He does not say for pagans, for idolaters, or for apostates, but among yourselves. <hi type="italic">Let brotherly love continue,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.13.1">Heb. xiii. 1</reference>. There is a special relation between all sincere Christians, and a particular amiableness and good in them, which require special affection. (2.) It is not enough for Christians not to bear malice, nor to have common respect for one another, they must intensely and fervently love each other. (3.) It is the property of true charity <hi type="italic">to cover a multitude of sins.</hi> It inclines people to forgive and forget offences against themselves, to cover and conceal the sins of others, rather than aggravate them and spread them abroad. It teaches us to love those who are but weak, and who have been guilty of many evil things before their conversion; and it prepares for mercy at the hand of God, who hath promised to forgive those that forgive others, <reference osisRef="Matt.6.14">Matt. vi. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen33492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33493" type="x-p"/> 3. To hospitality, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.9">v. 9</reference>. The hospitality here required is a free and kind entertainment of strangers and travellers. The proper objects of Christian hospitality are one another. The nearness of their relation, and the necessity of their condition in those times of persecution and distress, obliged Christians to be hospitable one to another. Sometimes Christians were spoiled of all they had, and were driven away to distant countries for safety. In this case they must starve if their fellow-christians would not receive them. Therefore it was a wise and necessary rule which the apostle here laid down. It is elsewhere commanded, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.1-Heb.13.2">Heb. xiii. 1, 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.12.13">Rom. xii. 13</reference>. The manner of performing this duty is this: it must be done in an easy, kind, handsome manner, <hi type="italic">without grudging</hi> or grumbling at the expense or trouble. Learn, (1.) Christians ought not only to be charitable, but hospitable, one to another. (2.) Whatever a Christian does by way of charity or of hospitality, he ought to do it cheerfully, and without grudging. <hi type="italic">Freely you have received, freely give.</hi> <div eID="gen33493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33494" type="x-p"/> 4. To the improvement of talents, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.11">v. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen33494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33495" type="x-p"/> (1.) The rule is that whatever gift, ordinary or extraordinary, whatever power, ability, or capacity of doing good is given to us, we should minister, or do service, with the same <hi type="italic">one to another,</hi> accounting ourselves not masters, but only <hi type="italic">stewards of the manifold grace,</hi> or the various gifts, of God. Learn, [1.] Whatever ability we have of doing good we must own it to be the gift of God and ascribe it to his grace. [2.] Whatever gifts we have received, we ought to look upon them as received for the use one of another. We must not assume them to ourselves, nor hide them in a napkin, but do service with them <hi type="italic">one to another</hi> in the best manner we are able. [3.] In receiving and using the manifold gifts of God we must look upon ourselves as stewards only, and act accordingly. The talents we are entrusted with are our Lord's goods, and must be employed as he directs. And it is required in a steward that he be found faithful. <div eID="gen33495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33496" type="x-p"/> (2.) The apostle exemplifies his direction about gifts in two particulars—speaking and ministering, concerning which he gives these rules:—[1.] <hi type="italic">If any man,</hi> whether a minister in public or a Christian in private conference, <hi type="italic">speak</hi> or teach, he must do it <hi type="italic">as the oracles of God,</hi> which direct us as to the matter of our speech. What Christians in private, or ministers in public, teach and speak must be the pure word and oracles of God. As to the manner of speaking, it must be with the seriousness, reverence, and solemnity, that become those holy and divine oracles. [2.] <hi type="italic">If any man minister,</hi> either as a deacon, distributing the alms of the church and taking care of the poor, or as a private person, by charitable gifts and contributions, <hi type="italic">let him do it as of the ability which God giveth.</hi> He who has received plenty and ability from God ought to minister plentifully, and according to his ability. These rules ought to be followed and practised for this end, <hi type="italic">that God in all things,</hi> in all your gifts, ministrations, and services, may be glorified, <hi type="italic">that others may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.16">Matt. v. 16</reference>), <hi type="italic">through Jesus Christ,</hi> who has procured and given these gifts to men (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.8">Eph. iv. 8</reference>), and through whom alone we and our services are accepted of God (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.15">Heb. xiii. 15</reference>), to whom, Jesus Christ, <hi type="italic">be praise and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.</hi> Learn, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is the duty of Christians in private, as well as ministers in public, to speak to one another of the things of God, <reference osisRef="Mal.3.16">Mal. iii. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.29">Eph. iv. 29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.145.10-Ps.145.12">Ps. cxlv. 10-12</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It highly concerns all preachers of the gospel to keep close to the word of God, and to treat that word as becomes the oracles of God. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Christians must not only do the duty of their place, but they must do it with vigour, and according to the best of their abilities. The nature of a Christian's work, which is high work and hard work, the goodness and kindness of the Master, and the excellency of the reward, all require that our endeavours should be serious and vigorous, and that whatever we are called to do for the honour of God and the good of others we should do it with all our might. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> In all the duties and services of life we should aim at the glory of God as our chief end; all other views must be subservient to this, which would sanctify our common actions and affairs, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.31">1 Cor. x. 31</reference>. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> God is not glorified by any thing we do if we do not offer it to him through the mediation and merits of Jesus Christ. <hi type="italic">God in all things must be glorified through Jesus Christ,</hi> who is the only way to the Father. <hi type="italic">Sixthly,</hi> The apostle's adoration of Jesus Christ, and ascribing unlimited and everlasting praise and dominion to him, prove that Jesus Christ is the most high God, over all blessed for evermore. Amen.
entries.129c7effaaf7a5493a7f86d6063cad4e5f43fdcc: <div eID="gen33496" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Fortitude and Circumspection; Advice to Suffering Christians. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen33497" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Beloved, think it not strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you, as though some strange thing happened unto you: <hi type="super">13</hi> But rejoice, inasmuch as ye are partakers of Christ's sufferings; that, when his glory shall be revealed, ye may be glad also with exceeding joy. <hi type="super">14</hi> If ye be reproached for the name of Christ, happy <hi type="italic">are ye;</hi> for the spirit of glory and of God resteth upon you: on their part he is evil spoken of, but on your part he is glorified. <hi type="super">15</hi> But let none of you suffer as a murderer, or <hi type="italic">as</hi> a thief, or <hi type="italic">as</hi> an evildoer, or as a busybody in other men's matters. 16 Yet if <hi type="italic">any man suffer</hi> as a Christian, let him not be ashamed; but let him glorify God on this behalf. <hi type="super">17</hi> For the time <hi type="italic">is come</hi> that judgment must begin at the house of God: and if <hi type="italic">it</hi> first <hi type="italic">begin</hi> at us, what shall the end <hi type="italic">be</hi> of them that obey not the gospel of God? <hi type="super">18</hi> And if the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear? <hi type="super">19</hi> Wherefore let them that suffer according to the will of God commit the keeping of their souls <hi type="italic">to him</hi> in well doing, as unto a faithful Creator. <div eID="gen33497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33498" type="x-p"/> The frequent repetition of counsel and comfort to Christians, considered as sufferers, in every chapter of this epistle, shows that the greatest danger these new converts were in arose from the persecutions to which their embracing Christianity exposed them. The good behaviour of Christians under sufferings is the most difficult part of their duty, but yet necessary both for the honour of Christ and their own comfort; and therefore the apostle, having extorted them in the former part of this chapter to the great duty of mortification, comes here to direct them in the necessary duty of patience under sufferings. An unmortified spirit is very unfit to bear trials. Observe, <div eID="gen33498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33499" type="x-p"/> I. The apostle's kind manner of address to these poor despised Christians: they were his <hi type="italic">beloved,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.9">v. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen33499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33500" type="x-p"/> II. His advice to them, relating to their sufferings, which is, <div eID="gen33500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33501" type="x-p"/> 1. That they should not think them strange, nor be surprised at them, as if some unexpected event befel them; for, <div eID="gen33501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33502" type="x-p"/> (1.) Though they be sharp and fiery, yet they are designed only to try, not to ruin them, to try their sincerity, strength, patience, and trust in God. On the contrary, they ought rather to rejoice under their sufferings, because theirs may properly be called Christ's sufferings. They are of the same kind, and for the same cause, that Christ suffered; they make us conformable to him; he suffers in them, and feels in our infirmities; and, if we be partakers of his sufferings, we shall also be make <hi type="italic">partakers of his glory,</hi> and shall meet him with exceeding joy at his great appearing to judge his enemies, and crown his faithful servants, <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.7">2 Thess. i. 7</reference>, &c. Learn, [1.] True Christians love and own the children of God in their lowest and most distressing circumstances. The apostle owns these poor afflicted Christians, and calls them his beloved. True Christians never look more amiable one to another than in their adversities. [2.] There is no reason for Christians to think strange, or to wonder, at the unkindnesses and persecutions of the world, because they are forewarned of them. Christ himself endured them; and forsaking all, denying ourselves, are the terms upon which Christ accepts of us to be his disciples. [3.] Christians ought not only to be patient, but to rejoice, in their sharpest sorest sufferings for Christ, because they are tokens of divine favour; they promote the gospel and prepare for glory. Those who rejoice in their sufferings for Christ shall eternally triumph and rejoice with him in glory. <div eID="gen33502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33503" type="x-p"/> (2.) From the fiery trial the apostle descends to a lower degree of persecution—that of the tongue by slander and reproach, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.14">v. 14</reference>. He supposes that this sort of suffering would fall to their lot: they would be reviled, evil-spoken of, and slandered for the name or sake of Christ. In such case he asserts, <hi type="italic">Happy are you,</hi> the reason of which is, "Because you have the spirit of God with you, to fortify and comfort you; and the Spirit of God is also the Spirit of glory, that will carry you through all, bring you off gloriously, and prepare and seal you up for eternal glory. This glorious Spirit <hi type="italic">resteth upon you,</hi> resideth with you, dwelleth in you, supporteth you, and is pleased with you; and is not this an unspeakable privilege? By your patience and fortitude in suffering, by your dependence upon the promises of God, and adhering to the word which the Holy Spirit hath revealed, <hi type="italic">he is on your part glorified;</hi> but by the contempt and reproaches cast upon you <hi type="italic">the Spirit itself</hi> is evil-spoken of and blasphemed." Learn, [1.] The best men and the best things usually meet with reproaches in the world. Jesus Christ and his followers, the Spirit of God and the gospel, are all evil-spoken of. [2.] The happiness of good people not only consists with, but even flows from their afflictions: <hi type="italic">Happy are you.</hi> [3.] That man who hath the Spirit of God resting upon him cannot be miserable, let his afflictions be ever so great: <hi type="italic">Happy are you; for the Spirit of God,</hi> &c. [4.] The blasphemies and reproaches which evil men cast upon good people are taken by the Spirit of God as cast upon himself: <hi type="italic">On their part he is evil-spoken of.</hi> [5.] When good people are vilified <hi type="italic">for the name of Christ</hi> his Holy Spirit is glorified in them. <div eID="gen33503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33504" type="x-p"/> 2. That they should take care they did not suffer justly, as evil-doers, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.15">v. 15</reference>. One would think such a caution as this needless to such an excellent set of Christians as these were. But their enemies charged them with these and other foul crimes: therefore the apostle, when he was settling the rules of the Christian religion, thought these cautions necessary, forbidding every one of them to hurt the life or the estate and property of any one, or to do any sort of evil, or, without call and necessity, to play the <hi type="italic">bishop in another man's charge,</hi> or busy himself <hi type="italic">in other men's matters.</hi> To this caution he adds a direction, <hi type="italic">that if any man suffer</hi> for the cause of Christianity, and with a patient Christian spirit, he ought not to account it a shame, but an honour to him; and ought to glorify God who hath thus dignified him, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.16">v. 16</reference>. Learn, (1.) The best of men need to be warned against the worst of sins. (2.) There is very little comfort in sufferings when we bring them upon ourselves by our own sin and folly. It is not the suffering, but the cause, that makes the martyr. (3.) We have reason to thank God for the honour if he calls us out to suffer for his truth and gospel, for our adherence to any of the doctrines or duties of Christianity. <div eID="gen33504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33505" type="x-p"/> 3. That their trials were now at hand, and they should stand prepared accordingly, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.17-1Pet.4.18">v. 17, 18</reference>. <div eID="gen33505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33506" type="x-p"/> (1.) He tells them that the time had come when <hi type="italic">judgment must begin at the house of God.</hi> The usual method of Providence has been this: When God brings great calamities and sore judgments upon whole nations, he generally begins with his own people, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.12">Isa. x. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.29">Jer. xxv. 29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.6">Ezek. ix. 6</reference>. "Such a time of universal calamity is now at hand, which was foretold by our Saviour, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.9-Matt.24.10">Matt. xxiv. 9, 10</reference>. This renders all the foregoing exhortations to patience necessary for you. And you have two considerations to support you." [1.] "That these judgments will but <hi type="italic">begin</hi> with you that are God's house and family, and will soon be over: your trials and corrections will not last long." [2.] "Your troubles will be but light and short, in comparison of what shall befal the wicked world, your own countrymen the Jews, and the infidels and idolatrous people among whom you live: <hi type="italic">What shall the end be of those who obey not the gospel of God?</hi>" Learn, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The best of God's servants, his own household, have so much amiss in them as renders it fit and necessary that God should sometimes correct and punish them with his judgments: <hi type="italic">Judgment begins at the house of God. Secondly,</hi> Those who are the family of God have their worst things in this life. Their worst condition is tolerable, and will soon be over. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Such persons or societies of men as <hi type="italic">disobey the gospel of God</hi> are not of his church and household, though possibly they may make the loudest pretensions. The apostle distinguishes the disobedient from the house of God. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> The sufferings of good people in this life are demonstrations of the unspeakable torments that are coming upon the disobedient and unbelieving: <hi type="italic">What shall the end be of those that obey not the gospel?</hi> Who can express or say how dreadful their end will be? <div eID="gen33506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33507" type="x-p"/> (2.) He intimates the irremediable doom of the wicked: <hi type="italic">If the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and sinner appear,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.18">v. 18</reference>. This whole verse is taken from <reference osisRef="Prov.11.31">Prov. xi. 31</reference>, <hi type="italic">Behold the righteous shall be recompensed in the earth; how much more the wicked and the sinner?</hi> This the LXX. translates exactly as the apostle here quotes it. Hence we may learn, [1.] The grievous sufferings of good people in this world are sad presages of much heavier judgments coming upon impenitent sinners. But, if we take the salvation here in the highest sense, then we may learn, [2.] It is as much as the best can do to secure the salvation of their souls; there are so many sufferings, temptations, and difficulties to be overcome, so many sins to be mortified, the gate is so strait and the way so narrow, that it is as much as the righteous can do to be saved. Let the absolute necessity of salvation balance the difficulty of it. Consider, Your difficulties are greatest at first; God offers his grace and help; the contest will not last long; be but faithful to the death, <hi type="italic">and God will give you the crown of life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.2.10">Rev. ii. 10</reference>. [3.] The ungodly and the sinner are unquestionably in a state of damnation. <hi type="italic">Where shall they appear?</hi> How will they stand before their Judge? Where can they show their heads? <hi type="italic">If the righteous scarcely be saved,</hi> the wicked must certainly perish. <div eID="gen33507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33508" type="x-p"/> 4. That when called to suffer, <hi type="italic">according to the will of God,</hi> they should look chiefly to the safety of their souls, which are put into hazard by affliction, and cannot be kept secure otherwise than by <hi type="italic">committing them to God,</hi> who will undertake the charge, if we commit them to him in well-doing; for he is their Creator, and has out of mere grace made many kind promises to them of eternal salvation, in which he will show himself faithful and true, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.19">v. 19</reference>. Learn, (1.) All the sufferings that befal good people come upon them <hi type="italic">according to the will of God.</hi> (2.) It is the duty of Christians, in all their distresses, to look more to the keeping of their souls than to the preserving of their bodies. The soul is of greatest value, and yet in most danger. If suffering from without raise uneasiness, vexation, and other sinful and tormenting passions within, the soul is then the greatest sufferer. If the soul be not well kept, persecution will drive people to apostasy, <reference osisRef="Ps.125.3">Ps. cxxv. 3</reference>. (3.) The only way to keep the soul well is to commit it to God, in well-doing. Commit your souls to God by solemn dedication, prayer, and patient perseverance in well-doing, <reference osisRef="Rom.2.7">Rom. ii. 7</reference>. (4.) Good people, when they are in affliction, have great encouragement to commit their souls to God, because he is their Creator, and faithful in all his promises.  <chapter eID="1Pet.4"/> <div eID="gen33508" type="x-p"/>

entries.3e413e7dca349ee49f5b6a0541fcebce7c98e3fb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18799"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <div sID="gen40089" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.1-1Pet.4.19">1Pe 4:1-19</reference>. Like the Risen Christ, Believers Henceforth Ought to Have No More to Do with Sin.<div eID="gen40089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40090" type="x-p"/> As the end is near, cultivate self-restraint, watchful prayerfulness, charity, hospitality, scriptural speech, ministering to one another according to your several gifts to the glory of God: Rejoicing patience under suffering.<div eID="gen40090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40091" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18799"/><hi type="bold">1. for us--</hi>supported by some oldest manuscripts and versions, omitted by others.<div eID="gen40091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40092" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the flesh--</hi>in His mortal body of humiliation.<div eID="gen40092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40093" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">arm--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eph.6.11">Ep 6:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.13">13</reference>).<div eID="gen40093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40094" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the same mind--</hi>of suffering with patient willingness what God wills you to suffer.<div eID="gen40094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40095" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he that hath suffered--</hi>for instance, Christ first, and in His person the believer: a general proposition.<div eID="gen40095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40096" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hath ceased--</hi>literally, "has been made to cease," has obtained by the very fact of His having suffered once for all, a cessation from sin, which had heretofore lain on Him (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.6-Rom.6.11">Ro 6:6-11</reference>, especially, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.7">1Pe 4:7</reference>). The Christian is by faith one with Christ: as then Christ by death is judicially freed from sin; so the Christian who has in the person of Christ died, has no more to do with it judicially, and ought to have no more to do with it actually. "The flesh" is the sphere in which sin has place. <div eID="gen40096" type="x-p"/>
entries.d91ab73f830ae95d70862e9b4953ba8833439aee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18800"/><div sID="gen40097" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18800"/><hi type="bold">2. That he, &c.--</hi>"That he (the believer, who has once for all obtained cessation from sin by suffering, in the person of Christ, namely, in virtue of his union with the crucified Christ) should no longer live the rest of his time in the flesh to the lusts of men, but to the will of God" as his rule. "Rest of his time in the flesh" (the Greek has the preposition "in" here, not in <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.1">1Pe 4:1</reference> as to Christ) proves that the reference is here not to Christ, but to the believer, whose remaining time for glorifying God is short (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.3">1Pe 4:3</reference>). "Live" in the truest sense, for heretofore he was dead. Not as Alford, "Arm yourselves ... with a view no longer to live the rest of your time." <div eID="gen40097" type="x-p"/>
entries.393b6f6e3df046947cf539d9f0e09a601aad934b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18801"/><div sID="gen40098" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18801"/><hi type="bold">3. may suffice--</hi>Greek, "is sufficient." Peter takes the lowest ground: for not even the past time ought to have been wasted in lust; but since you cannot recall it, at least lay out the future to better account.<div eID="gen40098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40099" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">us--</hi>omitted in oldest manuscripts.<div eID="gen40099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40100" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wrought--</hi>Greek, "wrought out."<div eID="gen40100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40101" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Gentiles--</hi>heathen: which many of you were.<div eID="gen40101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40102" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when, &c.--</hi>"walking as ye have done [Alford] in lasciviousness"; the Greek means petulant, immodest, wantonness, unbridled conduct: not so much filthy lust.<div eID="gen40102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40103" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">excess of wine--</hi>"wine-bibbings" [Alford].<div eID="gen40103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40104" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abominable--</hi>"nefarious," "lawless idolatries," violating God's most sacred law; not that all Peter's readers (see on <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.1">1Pe 1:1</reference>) walked in these, but many, namely, the Gentile portion of them. <div eID="gen40104" type="x-p"/>
entries.b2cfddc781c289401b1e44ce5b76ed588d02da1f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18802"/><div sID="gen40105" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18802"/><hi type="bold">4. Wherein--</hi>In respect to which abandonment of your former walk (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.3">1Pe 4:3</reference>).<div eID="gen40105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40106" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">run not with them--</hi>eagerly, in troops [Bengel].<div eID="gen40106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40107" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">excess--</hi>literally, "profusion"; a sink: stagnant water remaining after an inundation.<div eID="gen40107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40108" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">riot--</hi>profligacy.<div eID="gen40108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40109" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">speaking evil--</hi>charging you with pride, singularity, hypocrisy, and secret crimes (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.14">1Pe 4:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.2">2Pe 2:2</reference>). However, there is no "of you" in the Greek, but simply "blaspheming." It seems to me always to be used, either directly or indirectly, in the sense of impious reviling against God, Christ, or the Holy Spirit, and the Christian religion, not merely against men as such; Greek, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.14">1Pe 4:14</reference>, below. <div eID="gen40109" type="x-p"/>
entries.2ecaedc931c952803d360ec7b5270201095d6470: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18803"/><div sID="gen40110" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18803"/>5. They who now call you to account falsely, shall have to give account themselves for this very evil-speaking (Jude 15), and be condemned justly.<div eID="gen40110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40111" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ready--</hi>very speedily (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.7">1Pe 4:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.10">2Pe 3:10</reference>). Christ's coming is to the believer always near. <div eID="gen40111" type="x-p"/>
entries.23cc1361cf460b8b1755aa4bbbeffa717146703e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18804"/><div sID="gen40112" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18804"/><hi type="bold">6. For--</hi>giving the reason for <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.5">1Pe 4:5</reference>, "judge the dead."<div eID="gen40112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40113" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gospel preached also to ... dead--</hi>as well as to them now living, and to them that shall be found alive at the coming of the Judge. "Dead" must be taken in the same literal sense as in <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.5">1Pe 4:5</reference>, which refutes the explanation "dead" in sins. Moreover, the absence of the Greek article does not necessarily restrict the sense of "dead" to particular dead persons, for there is no Greek article in <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.5">1Pe 4:5</reference> also, where "the dead" is universal in meaning. The sense seems to be, Peter, as representing the true attitude of the Church in every age, expecting Christ at any moment, says, The Judge is ready to judge the quick and dead--the dead, I say, for they, too, in their lifetime, have had the Gospel preached to them, that so they might be judged at last in the same way as those living now (and those who shall be so when Christ shall come), namely, "men in the flesh," and that they might, having escaped condemnation by embracing the Gospel so preached, live unto God in the spirit (though death has passed over their flesh), <reference osisRef="Luke.20.38">Lu 20:38</reference>, thus being made like Christ in death and in life (see on <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.18">1Pe 3:18</reference>). He says, "live," not "made alive" or quickened; for they are supposed to have been already "quickened together with Christ" (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.5">Ep 2:5</reference>). This verse is parallel to <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.18">1Pe 3:18</reference>; compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.18">1Pe 3:18</reference>. The Gospel, substantially, was "preached" to the Old Testament Church; though not so fully as to the New Testament Church. It is no valid objection that the Gospel has not been preached to all that shall be found dead at Christ's coming. For Peter is plainly referring only to those within reach of the Gospel, or who might have known God through His ministers in Old and New Testament times. Peter, like Paul, argues that those found living at Christ's coming shall have no advantage above the dead who shall then be raised, inasmuch as the latter live unto, or "according to," God, even already in His purpose. Alford's explanation is wrong, "that they might be judged according to men as regards the flesh," that is, be in the state of the completed sentence on sin, which is death after the flesh. For "judged" cannot have a different meaning in this verse from what "judge" bears in <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.5">1Pe 4:5</reference>. "Live according to God" means, live a life with God, such as God lives, divine; as contrasted with "according to men in the flesh," that is, a life such as men live in the flesh. <div eID="gen40113" type="x-p"/>
entries.435954aa7a4e2391a249ff86dd38324f121adf37: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18805"/><div sID="gen40114" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18805"/>7. Resuming the idea in <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.5">1Pe 4:5</reference>.<div eID="gen40114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40115" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the end of all things--</hi>and therefore also of the wantonness (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.3">1Pe 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.4">4</reference>) of the wicked, and of the sufferings of the righteous [Bengel]. The nearness meant is not that of mere "time," but that before the Lord; as he explains to guard against misapprehension, and defends God from the charge of procrastination: We live in the last dispensation, not like the Jews under the Old Testament. The Lord will come as a thief; He is "ready" (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.5">1Pe 4:5</reference>) to judge the world at any moment; it is only God's long-suffering and His will that the Gospel should be preached as a witness to all nations, that induces Him to lengthen out the time which is with Him still as nothing.<div eID="gen40115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40116" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sober--</hi>"self-restrained." The opposite duties to the sins in <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.3">1Pe 4:3</reference> are here inculcated. Thus "sober" is the opposite of "lasciviousness" (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.3">1Pe 4:3</reference>).<div eID="gen40116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40117" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">watch--</hi>Greek, "be soberly vigilant"; not intoxicated with worldly cares and pleasures. Temperance promotes wakefulness or watchfulness, and both promote prayer. Drink makes drowsy, and drowsiness prevents prayer.<div eID="gen40117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40118" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prayer--</hi>Greek, "prayers"; the end for which we should exercise vigilance. <div eID="gen40118" type="x-p"/>
entries.bcda47ee439c3ce91174573b7866c7c85fe651b9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18806"/><div sID="gen40119" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18806"/><hi type="bold">8. above all things--</hi>not that "charity" or love is placed above "prayer," but because love is the animating spirit, without which all other duties are dead. Translate as Greek, "Having your mutual (literally, 'towards yourselves') charity intense." He presupposes its existence among them; he urges them to make it more fervent.<div eID="gen40119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40120" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">charity shall cover the multitude, &c.--</hi>The oldest manuscripts have "covereth." Quoted from <reference osisRef="Prov.10.12">Pr 10:12</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Prov.17.9">Pr 17:9</reference>. "Covereth" so as not harshly to condemn or expose faults; but forbearingly to bear the other's burdens, forgiving and forgetting past offenses. Perhaps the additional idea is included, By prayer for them, love tries to have them covered by God; and so being the instrument of converting the sinner from his error, "covereth a (not 'the,' as English Version) multitude of sins"; but the former idea from Proverbs is the prominent one. It is not, as Rome teaches, "covereth" his own sins; for then the Greek middle voice would be used; and <reference osisRef="Prov.10.12">Pr 10:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.17.9">17:9</reference> support the Protestant view. "As God with His love covers my sins if I believe, so must I also cover the sins of my neighbor" [Luther]. Compare the conduct of Shem and Japheth to Noah (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.23">Ge 9:23</reference>), in contrast to Ham's exposure of his father's shame. We ought to cover others' sins only where love itself does not require the contrary. <div eID="gen40120" type="x-p"/>
entries.46ddf15df1d86d8cc6e90347e342737d445cf156: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18807"/><div sID="gen40121" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18807"/>9. (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.13">Ro 12:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.2">He 13:2</reference>.) Not the spurious hospitality which passes current in the world, but the entertaining of those needing it, especially those exiled for the faith, as the representatives of Christ, and all hospitality to whomsoever exercised from genuine Christian love.<div eID="gen40121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40122" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without grudging--</hi>Greek, "murmuring." "He that giveth, let him do it with simplicity," that is open-hearted sincerity; with cordiality. Not secretly speaking against the person whom we entertain, or upbraiding him with the favor we have conferred in him. <div eID="gen40122" type="x-p"/>
entries.bb3b8e6996a6da90ef61f7cf56c8865dd40b8a02: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18808"/><div sID="gen40123" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18808"/><hi type="bold">10. every--</hi>"even as each man hath received," in whatever degree, and of whatever kind. The Spirit's gifts (literally, "gift of grace," that is, gratuitously bestowed) are the common property of the Christian community, each Christian being but a steward for the edifying of the whole, not receiving the gift merely for his own use.<div eID="gen40123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40124" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">minister the same--</hi>not discontentedly envying or disparaging the gift of another.<div eID="gen40124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40125" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one to another--</hi>Greek as in <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.8">1Pe 4:8</reference>, "towards yourselves"; implying that all form but one body, and in seeking the good of other members they are promoting the good of themselves.<div eID="gen40125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40126" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stewards--</hi>referring to <reference osisRef="Matt.25.15">Mt 25:15</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Luke.19.13-Luke.19.26">Lu 19:13-26</reference>. <div eID="gen40126" type="x-p"/>
entries.1c938bf4752ced071853dbaf5fd9b6f980e460de: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18809"/><div sID="gen40127" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18809"/><hi type="bold">11. If any ... speak--</hi>namely, as a prophet, or divinely taught teacher in the Church assembly.<div eID="gen40127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40128" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as the, &c.--</hi>The Greek has no article: "as oracles of God." This may be due to Greek: "God," having no article, it being a principle when a governed noun omits the Greek article that the governing noun should omit it, too. In <reference osisRef="Acts.7.38">Ac 7:38</reference> also, the Greek article is wanting; thus English Version, "as the oracles of God," namely, the Old Testament, would be "right," and the precept be similar to <reference osisRef="Rom.12.6">Ro 12:6</reference>, "prophesy according to the analogy of the faith." But the context suits better thus, "Let him speak as (becomes one speaking) oracles OF God." His divinely inspired words are not his own, but God's, and as a steward (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.10">1Pe 4:10</reference>) having them committed to him, he ought so to speak them. Jesus was the pattern in this respect (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.29">Mt 7:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.49">Joh 12:49</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.14.10">14:10</reference>; compare Paul, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.17">2Co 2:17</reference>). Note, the very same term as is applied in the only other passages where it occurs (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.38">Ac 7:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.3.2">Ro 3:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.5.12">He 5:12</reference>), to the Old Testament inspired writings, is here predicated of the inspired words (the substance of which was afterwards committed to writing) of the New Testament prophets.<div eID="gen40128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40129" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">minister--</hi>in acts; the other sphere of spiritual activity besides speaking.<div eID="gen40129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40130" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as of--</hi>"out of" the store of his "strength" (Greek, physical power in relation to outward service, rather than moral and intellectual "ability"; so in <reference osisRef="Mark.12.30">Mr 12:30</reference>).<div eID="gen40130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40131" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">giveth--</hi>Greek, "supplieth"; originally said of a choragus, who supplied the chorus with all necessaries for performing their several parts.<div eID="gen40131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40132" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that God in all things may be glorified--</hi>the final end of all a Christian's acts.<div eID="gen40132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40133" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through Jesus Christ--</hi>the mediator through whom all our blessings come down to us, and also through whom all our praises ascend to God. Through Christ alone can God be glorified in us and our sayings and doings.<div eID="gen40133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40134" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to whom--</hi>Christ.<div eID="gen40134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40135" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be--</hi>Greek, "is."<div eID="gen40135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40136" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for ever and ever--</hi>Greek, "unto the ages of the ages." <div eID="gen40136" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ef1175e0d3c78baeb201a54c571e6a2ad11eefb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18810"/><div sID="gen40137" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18810"/><hi type="bold">12. strange--</hi>they might think it strange that God should allow His chosen children to be sore tried.<div eID="gen40137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40138" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fiery trial--</hi>like the fire by which metals are tested and their dross removed. The Greek adds, "in your case."<div eID="gen40138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40139" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which is to try you--</hi>Greek, "which is taking place for a trial to you." Instead of its "happening to you" as some strange and untoward chance, it "is taking place" with the gracious design of trying you; God has a wise design in it--a consolatory reflection. <div eID="gen40139" type="x-p"/>
entries.65cae8824329e7ae653b7b552ee8fd7c7e99207c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18811"/><div sID="gen40140" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18811"/><hi type="bold">13. inasmuch as--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "in proportion as"; "in as far as" ye by suffering are partakers of Christ's sufferings, that is, by faith enter into realizing fellowship with them; willingly for His sake suffering as He suffered.<div eID="gen40140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40141" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with exceeding joy--</hi>Greek, "exulting joy"; now ye rejoice amidst sufferings; then ye shall EXULT, for ever free from sufferings (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.6">1Pe 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.8">8</reference>). If we will not bear suffering for Christ now, we must bear eternal sufferings hereafter. <div eID="gen40141" type="x-p"/>
entries.910337773b3e3cad05a1e86a6a4aca38498100ec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18812"/><div sID="gen40142" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18812"/><hi type="bold">14. for--</hi>Greek, "IN the name of Christ," namely, as Christians (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.16">1Pe 4:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.14">3:14</reference>, above); "in My name, because ye belong to Christ." The emphasis lies on this: <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.15">1Pe 4:15</reference>, "as a murderer, thief," &c., stands in contrast. Let your suffering be on account of Christ, not on account of evil-doing (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.20">1Pe 2:20</reference>).<div eID="gen40142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40143" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reproached--</hi>Reproach affects noble minds more than loss of goods, or even bodily sufferings.<div eID="gen40143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40144" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the spirit ... upon you--</hi>the same Spirit as rested on Christ (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.18">Lu 4:18</reference>). "The Spirit of glory" is His Spirit, for He is the "Lord of glory" (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.1">Jas 2:1</reference>). Believers may well overcome the "reproach" (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.11.26">He 11:26</reference>), seeing that "the Spirit of glory" rests upon them, as upon Him. It cannot prevent the happiness of the righteous, if they are reproached for Christ, because they retain before God their glory entire, as having the Spirit, with whom glory is inseparably joined [Calvin].<div eID="gen40144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40145" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and of God--</hi>Greek, "and the (Spirit) of God"; implying that the Spirit of glory (which is Christ's Spirit) is at the same time also the Spirit of God.<div eID="gen40145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40146" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">on their part he is evil spoken of, but on your part he is glorified--</hi>omitted in the two oldest Greek manuscripts and Syriac and Coptic versions, but supported by one very old manuscript, Vulgate, Sahidic, Cyprian, &c. "Evil spoken of," literally, "blasphemed"; not merely do they "speak against you," as in <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.16">1Pe 3:16</reference>, but blasphemously mock Christ and Christianity itself. <div eID="gen40146" type="x-p"/>
entries.1fed97c60c65e929b97235f6820ea1f2a8bb6703: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18813"/><div sID="gen40147" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18813"/><hi type="bold">15. But--</hi>Greek, "For." "Reproached in the name of Christ" I say (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.14">1Pe 4:14</reference>), "FOR let none," &c.<div eID="gen40147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40148" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as ... as ... as ... as--</hi>the "as" twice in italics is not in the Greek. The second Greek, "as," distinguishes the class "busybody in other men's matters," from the previous class of delinquents. Christians, from mistaken zeal, under the plea of faithfulness, might readily step out of their own calling and make themselves judges of the acts of unbelievers. Literally, "a bishop in what is (not his own, but) another's" province; an allusion to the existing bishops or overseers of the Church; a self-constituted bishop in others' concerns. <div eID="gen40148" type="x-p"/>
entries.e6e775d67df49b565a558fba93316a414f389dbd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18814"/><div sID="gen40149" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18814"/><hi type="bold">16. a Christian--</hi>the name given in contempt first at Antioch. <reference osisRef="Acts.11.26">Ac 11:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.26.28">26:28</reference>; the only three places where the term occurs. At first believers had no distinctive name, but were called among themselves "brethren," <reference osisRef="Acts.6.3">Ac 6:3</reference>; "disciples," <reference osisRef="Acts.6.1">Ac 6:1</reference>; "those of the way," <reference osisRef="Acts.9.2">Ac 9:2</reference>; "saints," <reference osisRef="Rom.1.7">Ro 1:7</reference>; by the Jews (who denied that Jesus was the Christ, and so would never originate the name Christian), in contempt, "Nazarenes." At Antioch, where first idolatrous Gentiles (Cornelius, <reference osisRef="Acts.10.1">Ac 10:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.2">2</reference>, was not an idolater, but a proselyte) were converted, and wide missionary work began, they could be no longer looked on as a Jewish sect, and so the Gentiles designated them by the new name "Christians." The rise of the new name marked a new epoch in the Church's life, a new stage of its development, namely, its missions to the Gentiles. The idle and witty people of Antioch, we know from heathen writers, were famous for inventing nicknames. The date of this Epistle must have been when this had become the generally recognized designation among Gentiles (it is never applied by Christians to each other, as it was in after ages--an undesigned proof that the New Testament was composed when it professes), and when the name exposed one to reproach and suffering, though not seemingly as yet to systematic persecution.<div eID="gen40149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40150" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let him not be ashamed--</hi>though the world is ashamed of shame. To suffer for one's own faults is no honor (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.15">1Pe 4:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.20">1Pe 2:20</reference>),--for Christ, is no shame (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.14">1Pe 4:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.13">1Pe 3:13</reference>).<div eID="gen40150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40151" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but let him glorify God--</hi>not merely glory in persecution; Peter might have said as the contrast, "but let him esteem it an honor to himself"; but the honor is to be given to God, who counts him worthy of such an honor, involving exemption from the coming judgments on the ungodly.<div eID="gen40151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40152" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">on this behalf--</hi>The oldest manuscripts and Vulgate read, "in this name," that is, in respect of suffering for such a name. <div eID="gen40152" type="x-p"/>
entries.3aa082546a08223bf728268f704ccd6d48927a62: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18815"/><div sID="gen40153" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18815"/>17. Another ground of consolation to Christians. All must pass under the judgment of God; God's own household first, their chastisement being here, for which they should glorify Him as a proof of their membership in His family, and a pledge of their escape from the end of those whom the last judgment shall find disobedient to the Gospel.<div eID="gen40153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40154" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the time--</hi>Greek, "season," "fit time."<div eID="gen40154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40155" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judgment must begin at the house of God--</hi>the Church of living believers. Peter has in mind <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.6">Eze 9:6</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Amos.3.2">Am 3:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.29">Jr 25:29</reference>. Judgment is already begun, the Gospel word, as a "two-edged sword," having the double effect of saving some and condemning others, and shall be consummated at the last judgment. "When power is given to the destroyer, he observes no distinction between the righteous and the wicked; not only so, but he begins first at the righteous" [Wetstein from Rabbins]. But God limits the destroyer's power over His people.<div eID="gen40155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40156" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if ... at us, what shall the end be of them, &c.--</hi>If even the godly have chastening judgments now, how much more shall the ungodly be doomed to damnatory judgments at last.<div eID="gen40156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40157" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gospel of God--</hi>the very God who is to judge them. <div eID="gen40157" type="x-p"/>
entries.34bc763503eb91b3025589cf2f3ad3414cd962a3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18816"/><div sID="gen40158" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18816"/><hi type="bold">18. scarcely--</hi>Compare "so as by fire," <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.15">1Co 3:15</reference>; having to pass through trying chastisements, as David did for his sin. "The righteous" man has always more or less of trial, but the issue is certain, and the entrance into the kingdom abundant at last. The "scarcely" marks the severity of the ordeal, and the unlikelihood (in a mere human point of view) of the righteous sustaining it; but the righteousness of Christ and God's everlasting covenant make it all sure.<div eID="gen40158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40159" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ungodly--</hi>having no regard for God; negative description.<div eID="gen40159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40160" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sinner--</hi>loving sin; positive; the same man is at once God-forgetting and sin-loving.<div eID="gen40160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40161" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">appear--</hi>in judgment. <div eID="gen40161" type="x-p"/>
entries.4f3bb9623427cb2e72323d7bc71958dee334e0f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18817"/><div sID="gen40162" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18817"/>19. General conclusion from <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.17">1Pe 4:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.18">18</reference>. Seeing that the godly know that their sufferings are by God's will, to chasten them that they may not perish with the world, they have good reason to trust God cheerfully amidst sufferings, persevering in well-doing.<div eID="gen40162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40163" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let them--</hi>Greek, "let them also," "let even them," as well as those not suffering. Not only under ordinary circumstances, but also in time of suffering, let believers commit. (Compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.14">1Pe 3:14</reference>).<div eID="gen40163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40164" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to the will of God--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.17">1Pe 3:17</reference>). God's will that the believer should suffer (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.17">1Pe 4:17</reference>), is for his good. One oldest manuscript and Vulgate read, "in well-doings"; contrast ill-doings, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.15">1Pe 4:15</reference>. Our committing of ourselves to God is to be, not in indolent and passive quietism, but accompanied with active well-doings.<div eID="gen40164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40165" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">faithful--</hi>to His covenant promises.<div eID="gen40165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40166" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Creator--</hi>who is therefore also our Almighty Preserver. He, not we, must keep our souls. Sin destroyed the original spiritual relation between creature and Creator, leaving that only of government. Faith restores it; so that the believer, living to the will of God (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.2">1Pe 4:2</reference>), rests implicitly on his Creator's faithfulness. <chapter eID="1Pet.4"/>

entries.1f5e6767b44be63977f282fb74951455fece1ef7: <div eID="gen54645" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen54646" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen54647" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen54647" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen54646" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen54648" type="x-p"/> We should suffer patiently, after the example of Christ, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.1">1Pet 4:1</reference>. And no longer live according to our former custom, but disregard the scoffs of those who are incensed against us because we have forsaken their evil ways, who are shortly to give account to God for their conduct, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.2-1Pet.4.5">1Pet 4:2-5</reference>. How the Gospel was preached to Jews and Gentiles, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.6">1Pet 4:6</reference>. As the end of all things was at hand, they should be sober, watchful, charitable, benevolent, good stewards of the bounty of Providence; and, when called to instruct others, speak as the oracles of God, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.7-1Pet.4.11">1Pet 4:7-11</reference>. Of the persecutions and trials which were coming upon them, and how they were to suffer so as not to disgrace their Christian character, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.12-1Pet.4.16">1Pet 4:12-16</reference>. Judgment was about to begin at the house of God, and even the righteous would escape with difficulty from the calamities coming upon the Jews; but they must continue in well-doing, and thus commit the keeping of their souls to their faithful Creator, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.17-1Pet.4.19">1Pet 4:17-19</reference>. <div eID="gen54648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54649" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen54649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54650" type="x-p"/> As Christ hath suffered - He is your proper pattern; have the same disposition he had; the same forgiving spirit, with meekness, gentleness, and complete self-possession. <div eID="gen54650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54651" type="x-p"/> He that hath suffered in the flesh, hath ceased from sin - This is a general maxim, if understood literally: The man who suffers generally reflects on his ways, is humbled, fears approaching death, loathes himself because of his past iniquities, and ceases from them; for, in a state of suffering, the mind loses its relish for the sins of the flesh, because they are embittered to him through the apprehension which he has of death and judgment; and, on his application to God's mercy, he is delivered from his sin. <div eID="gen54651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54652" type="x-p"/> Some suppose the words are to be understood thus: "Those who have firmly resolved, if called to it, to suffer death rather than apostatize from Christianity, have consequently ceased from, or are delivered from, the sin of saving their lives at the expense of their faith." Others think that it is a parallel passage to <reference osisRef="Rom.6.7">Rom 6:7</reference>, and interpret it thus: "He that hath mortified the flesh, hath ceased from sin." Dr. Bentley applies the whole to our redemption by Christ: He that hath suffered in the flesh hath died for our sins. But this seems a very constrained sense.
entries.2c3796b54d94a7c4b7f11275f650197fea3d1cc0: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen54652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54653" type="x-p"/> That he no longer should live - in the flesh - Governed by the base principle of giving up his faith to save his life; to the lusts of men - according to the will of his idolatrous persecutors; but to the will of God; which will of God is, that he should retain the truth, and live according to its dictates, though he should suffer for it.
entries.076139a14c7a6a05450a3e38e72f9329af8cfaa8: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen54653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54654" type="x-p"/> The time past of our life - This is a complete epitome of the Gentile or heathen state, and a proof that those had been Gentiles to whom the apostle wrote. <div eID="gen54654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54655" type="x-p"/> 1. They walked in lasciviousness, εν ασελγειαις· every species of lechery, lewdness, and impurity. <div eID="gen54655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54656" type="x-p"/> 2. In lusts, επιθυμιαις· strong irregular appetites, and desires of all kinds. <div eID="gen54656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54657" type="x-p"/> 3. In excess of wine, οινοφλυγιαις· wine, and φλυω, to be hot, or to boil; to be inflamed with wine; they were in continual debauches. <div eID="gen54657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54658" type="x-p"/> 4. In revellings, κωμοις· lascivious feastings, with drunken songs, etc. See the note on <reference osisRef="Rom.13.13">Rom 13:13</reference>. <div eID="gen54658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54659" type="x-p"/> 5. In banquetings, ποτοις· wine feasts, drinking matches, etc. <div eID="gen54659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54660" type="x-p"/> 6. In abominable idolatries, αθεμιτοις ειδωλολατρειαις· that is, the abominations practised at their idol feasts, where they not only worshipped the idol, but did it with the most impure, obscene, and abominable rites. <div eID="gen54660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54661" type="x-p"/> This was the general state of the Gentile world; and with this monstrous wickedness Christianity had everywhere to struggle.
entries.a564341c8dcccc5590386acef3aa9e1b2cde017c: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen54661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54662" type="x-p"/> They think it strange - Ξενιζονται· They wonder and are astonished at you, that ye can renounce these gratifications of the flesh for a spiritual something, the good of which they cannot see. <div eID="gen54662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54663" type="x-p"/> Excess of riot - Ασωτιας αναχυσιν· Flood of profligacy; bearing down all rule, order, and restraints before it. <div eID="gen54663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54664" type="x-p"/> Speaking evil of you - Βλασφημουντες· Literally, blaspheming; i.e. speaking impiously against God, and calumniously of you.
entries.2176c2d70e4f7550f5f43573f40191f5d29836f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen54664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54665" type="x-p"/> To judge the quick and the dead - They shall give account of these irregularities to Him who is prepared to judge both the Jews and the Gentiles. The Gentiles, previously to the preaching of the Gospel among them, were reckoned to be dead in trespasses and sins, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.1-Eph.2.5">Eph 2:1-5</reference>; under the sentence of death, because they had sinned. The Jews had at least, by their religious profession, a name to live; and by that profession were bound to give to God.
entries.e59daa890438a0dd4f88197837d47235f49c783c: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen54665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54666" type="x-p"/> Was the Gospel preached also to them that are dead - This is a most difficult verse; the best translations I have seen of it are the following: - "For this indeed was the effect of the preaching of the Gospel to the dead, (the unconverted Gentiles), that some will be punished as carnal men; but others, (those converted to Christianity), lead a spiritual life unto God." - Wakefield. "For this purpose hath the Gospel been preached even to the dead, (i.e. the Gentiles), that although they might be condemned, indeed, by men in the flesh, (their persecutors), yet they might live eternally by God in the Spirit." - Macknight. "For this cause was the Gospel preached to them that were dead; that they who live according to men in the flesh, may be condemned; but that they who live according to God in the Spirit, may live." - Knatchbull. <div eID="gen54666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54667" type="x-p"/> There are as many different translations of this verse, and comments upon it, as there are translators and commentators. That of Sir Norton Knatchbull, could the Greek text bear it, appears the most simple; but that of Dr. Macknight, which is nearly the sense given by Mr. Wesley in his Paraphrase, is more likely to be the true one among those already proposed. <div eID="gen54667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54668" type="x-p"/> But if the apostle had the same fact in view which he mentions, <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.19">1Pet 3:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.20">1Pet 3:20</reference>, then the antediluvians are the persons intended: For this cause - that Christ is prepared to judge the quick and the dead, and to dispense righteous judgment in consequence of having afforded them every necessary advantage, was the Gospel preached by Noah to them also who are dead - the antediluvian world, then dead in trespasses and sins, and condemned to death by the righteous judgment of God; but in his great compassion he afforded them a respite, that though they were condemned as men in the flesh, (for this was their character; my Spirit will not always strive with man, forasmuch as he is Flesh, <reference osisRef="Gen.6.3">Gen 6:3</reference>), yet, hearing this Gospel by Noah, they may believe, and live according to God in the Spirit - live a blessed life in eternity according to the mercy of God, who sent his Spirit to strive with them. This appears to me to be the most consistent sense; especially as the apostle seems to refer to what he had said of the Spirit of Christ in Noah preaching to the spirits in prison - the rebellions that lived before the flood.
